arXiv:2605.30335v1 [cs.AI] 28 May 2026

Locally Coherent, Globally Incoherent:
Bounding Compositional Incoherence in Multi-Component LLM Agents

Anany Kotawala Affiliation: Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA Correspondence to: akotawala@princeton.edu
Abstract

Multi-component LLM agents assemble probabilistic claims from components that each see only part of a joint problem; the composition can violate basic probability axioms even when every component is locally coherent. We formalise this locally coherent, globally incoherent failure via the compositional residual ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}, the L2L_{2} distance from the composed quote to the joint coherent polytope, computable at runtime from system output and the declared cross-component coupling constraints. A product-structure dichotomy characterises when local coherence suffices, and a Rayleigh-quotient prediction matches the observed residual within 7%7\% on three of four relation classes. A hierarchical Boyle–Dykstra projection repairs the composition deterministically; an anytime-valid e-process gives sequential coherence monitoring. Across 1,8761{,}876 ensemble cliques on a four-LLM mid-tier panel (frontier-panel rerun in §5.5), ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 3333–94%94\% of cliques, translating to +0.115+0.115 nats per bet of regret on 1,7701{,}770 resolved bets under the proportional allocation rule (the gain collapses to +0.006+0.006 under bettors that themselves coherentise). Three intuitive LLM-side mitigations (retrieval, partition-aware prompting, aggregator-LLM) each fail or regress.

Keywords: 
foundation models, compositional generalization, formal performance guarantees, decomposable benchmark, instance-wise uncertainty, calibration, hierarchical projection, FTAP, anytime-valid inference, Brier score, multi-component systems

1 Introduction

Foundation-model evaluation routinely reports per-question accuracy, calibration, and proper-scoring statistics; formal, instance-wise guarantees on system-level performance under composition of multiple model calls are comparatively scarce. In multi-component agents, planners route retrieval, arithmetic, and probability assessment to specialist subagents or tools, and each component handles only part of a joint question. Even when every component is calibrated and internally coherent on its assigned questions, the aggregated belief need not be: a research component emitting P⁡(Republican)=0.6P(\text{Republican}){=}0.6 and a forecasting component emitting P⁡(Democrat)=0.6P(\text{Democrat}){=}0.6 produce a 1.21.2-mass quote that no probability measure can assign, inducing a Dutch-book exposure (de Finetti, 1937) that arises strictly between components. Per-component coherence does not, in general, repair the composed system; we call this regime locally coherent, globally incoherent; Figure 1 shows a concrete instance from the planner-discretion harness of §5.3.

Per-component calibration, self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), and conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021) act on individual model outputs and preserve only per-output coherence properties; cross-component logical constraints are invisible to all three. We identify the compositional residual ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}, the L2L_{2} distance from the composed quote to the joint coherent polytope, as a runtime, distribution-free certificate of system-level coherence under owner-selected aggregation; it is computable from the composed quote and the cross-component constraints alone. As a constructive repair preserving specialist routing, we use a hierarchical Boyle–Dykstra projection. We pair these with closed-form bounds, an anytime-valid sequential test, and a decomposable benchmark whose hardness is predicted by the theory.

A product-structure dichotomy (Theorem 3.3) characterises when local coherence suffices: under owner-selected aggregation (each component owns a subset of joint coordinates; the aggregator just selects what each owner already wrote), component coherence guarantees system coherence for all inputs if and only if the joint polytope factorises as a Cartesian product of local polytopes. Under any tighter coupling, locally coherent component forecasts exist whose composition is globally incoherent, and ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} certifies this failure mode (Cor. 3.4). Cor. 3.9 converts the existential dichotomy into a closed-form magnitude prediction (Rayleigh-quotient form) computable from the specialist panel covariance alone.

Operationally, ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} yields a bound Exposure⋆≤m⋆​ε⋆\mathrm{Exposure}^{\star}\!\leq\!\sqrt{m^{\star}}\,\varepsilon^{\star} (Cor. 3.5) on system-level Dutch-book exposure under the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP); the hierarchical Boyle–Dykstra repair (Theorem 3.10) drives this bound to the numerical floor, and the corresponding e-process (a sequential test controlling false positives at any stopping time) gives an anytime-valid coherence test (§3.7, Theorem D.2). The convex-analytic machinery is classical; the contribution is the operational reframing of ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} as a runtime certificate, the dichotomy of Theorem 3.3, the falsifiable magnitude prediction of Cor. 3.9, and the decomposable benchmark whose hardness ordering the theory predicts.

Empirically, we evaluate 1,8761{,}876 ensemble cliques drawn from Paleka (Paleka et al., 2025) and Polymarket across four contemporary foundation models, stratified by four logical-relation classes. The empirical hardness ordering (partition >> negation >> disjunction >> conjunction) tracks how tightly each polytope constrains the joint quote, as predicted by Theorem 3.3, and Cor. 3.9’s magnitude prediction matches the observed expected residual within 7%7\% on three of the four relation classes (the conjunction under-shoot at ×0.83\!\times is itself predicted by the Cor. 3.9 interior-Π¯\bar{\Pi} regime). The exposure bound m⋆​ε⋆\sqrt{m^{\star}}\varepsilon^{\star} averages 0.1370.137 under naive composition (Figure 2b) and is reduced to the QP solver floor by hierarchical projection. We report per-cell Brier with Diebold–Mariano significance (the standard paired test for forecast comparison), and validate with a same-model decoupling control, leakage filtering, and a tool-augmented A/B; full protocols and a reproducibility manifest are in the appendices.

2 Preliminaries

Throughout, starred objects denote the composed system, while subscripts denote individual components.

Cliques and the coherent polytope.

A clique CC is a tuple (Q1,…,Qm,R)(Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},R) of mm Bernoulli questions and logical relations RR. By de Finetti (1937), the set ℳC={r∈[0,1]m:∃μ∈Δ⁡({0,1}m)​consistent with ​R}\mathcal{M}_{C}=\{r\in[0,1]^{m}:\exists\,\mu\in\Delta(\{0,1\}^{m})\ \text{consistent with }R\} is a closed convex polytope. We denote the L2L_{2} projection ΠC:[0,1]m→ℳC\Pi_{C}:[0,1]^{m}\to\mathcal{M}_{C} and the residual εC​(p^):=‖p^−ΠC​(p^)‖2\varepsilon_{C}(\hat{p}):=\|\hat{p}-\Pi_{C}(\hat{p})\|_{2}.

KK-sample empirical marginal.

A forecaster supplies KK i.i.d. samples per question, yielding p^∈[0,1]m\hat{p}\in[0,1]^{m} with p^j=K−1​∑kYj,k\hat{p}_{j}=K^{-1}\sum_{k}Y_{j,k} and population limit pF:=limK→∞p^p_{F}:=\lim_{K\to\infty}\hat{p}. Generically p^∉ℳC\hat{p}\notin\mathcal{M}_{C} even when pF∈ℳCp_{F}\in\mathcal{M}_{C} (due to finite-sample fluctuation).

Within-component JCD.

Joint-Coherent Decoding is the L2L_{2} projection of KK-sample LLM marginals onto the local coherent polytope ℳC\mathcal{M}_{C}. The compositional layer treats JCD as the local repair operator; it inherits a Pythagorean Brier improvement (Theorem A.1, App. A) and a finite-state no-Dutch-book bound via the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP; Cor. A.2) bounded by m⋅εKKT≤×10−5m\cdot\varepsilon^{\mathrm{KKT}}\!\leq\!1.4\!\times\!10^{-5} at the default tolerance of OSQP, the quadratic-program solver we use throughout.

Multi-component agent.

The agent has kk sub-models indexed by a∈[k]a\in[k]. Sub-model aa emits an empirical marginal p^(a)∈[0,1]ma\hat{p}^{(a)}\in[0,1]^{m_{a}} on its local question set 𝒬a\mathcal{Q}_{a} with local polytope ℳa⊆[0,1]ma\mathcal{M}_{a}\subseteq[0,1]^{m_{a}}; component-level JCD produces Πa​(p^(a))∈ℳa\Pi_{a}(\hat{p}^{(a)})\in\mathcal{M}_{a}. The agent’s joint question set is 𝒬⋆=⋃a𝒬a\mathcal{Q}^{\star}=\bigcup_{a}\mathcal{Q}_{a} with size m⋆=|𝒬⋆|m^{\star}=|\mathcal{Q}^{\star}| and joint polytope ℳ⋆⊆[0,1]m⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}\subseteq[0,1]^{m^{\star}}, which respects (i) each local relation lifted to 𝒬⋆\mathcal{Q}^{\star} and (ii) all cross-component coupling constraints 𝒞\mathcal{C}: identifications of shared questions, cross-component logical relations like Q⋆=Qa∧QbQ^{\star}=Q_{a}\wedge Q_{b}, and partitions spanning components.

Aggregator.

An aggregator 𝒜:∏a[0,1]ma→[0,1]m⋆\mathcal{A}:\prod_{a}[0,1]^{m_{a}}\to[0,1]^{m^{\star}} assembles the agent’s quoted marginal vector. The aggregator 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the owner-selected coordinate selector of Definition 3.2; this covers the specialist-routing and tool-call composition patterns used in our experiments. We focus on owner-selection because it is the practical pattern under compute budgets: each component owns a subset of joint coordinates and there is no redundant elicitation across specialists. A coord-wise averaging aggregator 𝒜avg​(Π1,…,Πk)=k−1​∑aΠa\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{avg}}(\Pi_{1},\dots,\Pi_{k})=k^{-1}\sum_{a}\Pi_{a} on the same inputs would already lie in ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} by convexity, so the failure mode of Theorem 3.3 is structurally absent under averaging; we verify this empirically (Section 4). The cost of averaging is k×k\times elicitation per coordinate, which is the regime specialist-routing is designed to avoid.

The two candidate workflows.

With p^=(p^(1),…,p^(k))\hat{p}=(\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\hat{p}^{(k)}) and the aggregator 𝒜\mathcal{A} fixed, two natural projections into ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} arise:

Local-then-global: Π⋆​(𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))),\displaystyle\Pi^{\star}(\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)})), (1)
Direct global: Π⋆​(𝒜⁡(p^(1),…,p^(k))).\displaystyle\Pi^{\star}(\mathcal{A}(\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\hat{p}^{(k)})). (2)

The substantive question is when, and by how much, these differ.

3 Method

Throughout this section we assume the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is explicitly specified; the regime of implicit 𝒞\mathcal{C} recovered from agent transcripts is discussed in §6.

3.1 When local coherence composes

Definition 3.1 (Compositional residual).

For inputs p^=(p^(1),…,p^(k))\hat{p}=(\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\hat{p}^{(k)}) and aggregator 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the compositional residual is

ε⋆(p^):=∥\displaystyle\varepsilon^{\star}(\hat{p})\;:=\;\bigl\| 𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)})
−Π⋆(𝒜(Π1p^(1),…,Πkp^(k)))∥2.\displaystyle-\Pi^{\star}\!\bigl(\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)})\bigr)\bigr\|_{2}.

It is the L2L_{2} distance from the locally-repaired composed quote to the joint coherent polytope ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}.

Lifted local feasible sets.

For each component aa, lift ℳa⊆[0,1]ma\mathcal{M}_{a}\subseteq[0,1]^{m_{a}} to ℳa↑⊆[0,1]m⋆\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\uparrow}\subseteq[0,1]^{m^{\star}} by leaving the non-component coordinates free. Write ℳ⊠:=⋂aℳa↑\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}:=\bigcap_{a}\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\uparrow} for the joint feasibility implied by the local constraints alone (no cross-component coupling). ℳ⋆⊆ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}\subseteq\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes} always; equality holds iff the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is trivial.

Definition 3.2 (Owner-selected aggregation).

Fix the joint question set 𝒬⋆\mathcal{Q}^{\star}. An ownership map owner:𝒬⋆→[k]\mathrm{owner}:\mathcal{Q}^{\star}\!\to\![k] assigns each joint coordinate to a single component. If multiple components originally quote the same question jj, we keep separate local coordinates pa,jp_{a,j} and pb,jp_{b,j} in the product input space before owner selection, and record the equality pa,j=pb,jp_{a,j}=p_{b,j} in the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The aggregator 𝒜\mathcal{A} selects the coordinate owned by owner⁡(j)\mathrm{owner}(j). Aggregation only selects; coupling enforces agreement.

Theorem 3.3 (Product-structure dichotomy).

Under owner-selected coordinate aggregation 𝒜\mathcal{A}, local coherence guarantees global coherence for all inputs p^\hat{p} if and only if ℳ⋆=ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}=\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}. When ℳ⋆=ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}=\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, projection decomposes blockwise:

Π⋆​(𝒜⁡(p^(1),…,p^(k)))=𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k)),\Pi^{\star}(\mathcal{A}(\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\hat{p}^{(k)}))=\mathcal{A}\bigl(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)}\bigr), (3)

so ε⋆≡0\varepsilon^{\star}\equiv 0. When ℳ⋆⊊ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}\subsetneq\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, there exists r∈ℳ⊠∖ℳ⋆r\in\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}\setminus\mathcal{M}^{\star}, and locally coherent component forecasts realizing rr yield a composed quote with ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}>0.

Proof (forward).

If ℳ⋆=ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}=\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, the squared L2L_{2} norm decomposes: ‖p^−r‖2=∑a‖p^(a)−r(a)‖2\|\hat{p}-r\|^{2}=\sum_{a}\|\hat{p}^{(a)}-r^{(a)}\|^{2} for any r∈ℳ⊠r\in\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, so the joint minimization separates into kk independent local minimizations. Hence Π⋆​(p^)=(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))\Pi^{\star}(\hat{p})=(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)}) which equals the aggregator’s output on this product space, and ε⋆≡0\varepsilon^{\star}\equiv 0. This is the block-product structure of L2L_{2} projection in Hilbert space (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017, Prop. 29.3). ∎

Proof (reverse, existential).

Take any r∈ℳ⊠∖ℳ⋆r\in\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}\setminus\mathcal{M}^{\star} and lift it to component restrictions; owner-selection then reassembles rr from locally coherent inputs, and r∉ℳ⋆r\notin\mathcal{M}^{\star} closed gives ε⋆=‖r−Π⋆​(r)‖2>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!=\!\|r-\Pi^{\star}(r)\|_{2}\!>\!0. Full construction in App. B. ∎

The forward direction is the block-product factorization of L2L_{2} projection in Hilbert space (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017, Prop. 29.3); the contribution is operational, identifying when local coherence is sufficient and when ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} is an appropriate online certificate. We also refer to Theorem 3.3 as the non-commutation theorem, since it characterizes exactly when local-then-global L2L_{2} projection commutes with the aggregator (and when it does not). The reverse direction is existential: it shows local coherence is not sufficient under coupling, but does not characterize the typical magnitude of ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}. Section 5 estimates this empirically.

Corollary 3.4 (Zero-residual characterization).

Even under coupling, ε⋆=0\varepsilon^{\star}=0 if and only if 𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))∈ℳ⋆\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)})\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}. The compositional certificate is positive on a given input exactly when local repairs do not satisfy the cross-component constraints.

Proof.

Π⋆\Pi^{\star} is the identity on ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} by definition; ‖x−Π⋆​(x)‖2=0\|x-\Pi^{\star}(x)\|_{2}=0 iff x∈ℳ⋆x\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}. ∎

3.2 Exposure interpretation

Corollary 3.5 (System-level FTAP exposure bound).

Treat the coordinates of 𝒜⁡(Π1,…,Πk)\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1},\dots,\Pi_{k}) as quoted unit-pay prices on the m⋆m^{\star} Bernoulli contracts of the joint clique C⋆C^{\star}. If ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}>0, the finite-state FTAP yields a Dutch-book portfolio against the joint quote. Moreover, under the unit-stake Logarithmic Market Scoring Rule (LMSR; Hanson, 2003) exposure statistic used in our experiments, Exposure⋆≤m⋆​ε⋆.\mathrm{Exposure}^{\star}\leq\sqrt{m^{\star}}\,\varepsilon^{\star}. Every individual sub-model’s component-level Dutch-book exposure is zero by construction up to the QP tolerance (since Πa​(p^(a))∈ℳa\Pi_{a}(\hat{p}^{(a)})\in\mathcal{M}_{a}); any positive joint exposure is therefore attributable to cross-component incoherence, modulo the numerical solver floor.

Proof.

If the quoted vector lies outside ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}, the separating hyperplane form of de Finetti’s finite-state FTAP gives a portfolio with nonnegative payoff in every coherent state and strictly positive price discrepancy. For the relation classes used in our experiments, the unit-stake exposure statistic is the positive violation of a defining halfspace (or a sum of mutually exclusive positive violations). If h⁡(x)=(⟨a,x⟩−b)+h(x)=(\langle a,x\rangle-b)_{+} is any such violation and xΠ=Π⋆​(x)x^{\Pi}=\Pi^{\star}(x), then h⁡(x)≤|⟨a,x−xΠ⟩|≤‖a‖2​‖x−xΠ‖2h(x)\leq|\langle a,x-x^{\Pi}\rangle|\leq\|a\|_{2}\|x-x^{\Pi}\|_{2}. For negation, conjunction, disjunction, and partition constraints ‖a‖2≤m⋆\|a\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{m^{\star}} after the relation is embedded in the m⋆m^{\star} joint coordinate system, yielding Exposure⋆≤m⋆​ε⋆\mathrm{Exposure}^{\star}\leq\sqrt{m^{\star}}\varepsilon^{\star}. Each Πa​(p^(a))∈ℳa\Pi_{a}(\hat{p}^{(a)})\in\mathcal{M}_{a} has zero local residual to ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} by definition, so the per-component exposure diagnostic is zero up to numerical solver tolerance. ∎

Corollary 3.6 (System-level Pythagorean Brier improvement).

Let p⋆∈ℳ⋆p^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} be the true joint marginal vector and let rr be any composed quote. Then ‖Π⋆​(r)−p⋆‖22≤‖r−p⋆‖22−‖r−Π⋆​(r)‖22.\|\Pi^{\star}(r)-p^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}\;\leq\;\|r-p^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}-\|r-\Pi^{\star}(r)\|_{2}^{2}. In particular, taking r=𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))r=\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)}) yields a deterministic, sample-path Brier-improvement guarantee for hierarchical JCD whose slack ‖r−Π⋆​(r)‖22=(ε⋆)2\|r-\Pi^{\star}(r)\|_{2}^{2}=(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2} is largest exactly where the compositional residual is largest.

Proof.

The Hilbert-projection argument of Theorem A.1 applied to Π⋆\Pi^{\star} on ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}. ∎

Corollary 3.7 (Brier lift under {0,1}\{0,1\} labels: condition and reversal).

Let y∈{0,1}m⋆y\!\in\!\{0,1\}^{m^{\star}} be a resolved label vector and let p⋆:=𝔼⁡[y]p^{\star}:=\mathbb{E}[y] denote the true marginal. For any composed quote rr, 𝔼y​[Brier⁡(r,y)−Brier⁡(Π⋆​(r),y)]=‖r−p⋆‖22−‖Π⋆​(r)−p⋆‖22.\mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathrm{Brier}(r,y)-\mathrm{Brier}(\Pi^{\star}(r),y)]\;=\;\|r-p^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\Pi^{\star}(r)-p^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}. If p⋆∈ℳ⋆p^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}, this difference is at least ‖r−Π⋆​(r)‖22=(ε⋆)2≥0\|r-\Pi^{\star}(r)\|_{2}^{2}=(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}\geq 0 by Cor. 3.6; hierarchical JCD improves expected Brier (in expectation over yy; the sample-path geometric bound is Cor. 3.6). If p⋆∉ℳ⋆p^{\star}\notin\mathcal{M}^{\star} (label incoherence: a fraction of resolutions violate the assumed logical structure), the difference can be negative; projection can amplify the error against p⋆p^{\star}.

The condition p⋆∈ℳ⋆p^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} is the precise assumption under which Cor. 3.6 transfers from the geometric to the predictive setting. Empirically (§5), the lift holds with p<10−15p\!<\!10^{-15} on negation, conjunction, and partition; on disjunction the gain is borderline (Δ​Brier=+0.0027\Delta\mathrm{Brier}\!=\!{+}0.0027, p=0.07p\!=\!0.07), diagnosing a small fraction of disjunction cliques whose resolved labels deviate from the strict A∨BA\!\vee\!B relation: this is exactly the p⋆∉ℳ⋆p^{\star}\!\notin\!\mathcal{M}^{\star} regime in which Cor. 3.7 predicts the lift can reverse.

3.3 Disagreement controls the residual

Proposition 3.8 (Disagreement upper bound on ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}).

Let r∈ℳ⋆r\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} be any globally coherent reference forecast, that is, any joint quote that already lies in the joint polytope. Under owner-selected coordinate aggregation,

ε⋆​(p^)≤‖𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))−r‖2.\varepsilon^{\star}(\hat{p})\;\leq\;\bigl\|\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)})-r\bigr\|_{2}.

A natural choice for rr is the JCD-projected forecast Πβ​(p^(β))\Pi_{\beta}(\hat{p}^{(\beta)}) of any component β\beta that itself lies in ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}, for instance a component routed the entire joint clique. The right-hand side is then the L2L_{2} disagreement between the composed quote and the reference. It vanishes when all coordinates are assigned to the same component, so inter-component disagreement on disputed coordinates is a measurable proxy that both explains and upper-bounds the residual.

Proof.

By the variational characterization of L2L_{2} projection onto a closed convex set, ε⋆=‖x−Π⋆​(x)‖2≤‖x−r‖2\varepsilon^{\star}=\|x-\Pi^{\star}(x)\|_{2}\leq\|x-r\|_{2} for any r∈ℳ⋆r\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}, where x=𝒜⁡(Π1​p^(1),…,Πk​p^(k))x=\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1}\hat{p}^{(1)},\dots,\Pi_{k}\hat{p}^{(k)}). ∎

Let Δj\Delta_{j} denote the per-coordinate disagreement between the assigned LLM and a globally-coherent reference β\beta. For each relation class the bound takes a closed form keyed to the constraint normal: |Δ1+Δ2|/2|\Delta_{1}{+}\Delta_{2}|/\sqrt{2} on negation, |∑jΔj|/m⋆|\sum_{j}\Delta_{j}|/\sqrt{m^{\star}} on partition, and ‖Δ‖2\|\Delta\|_{2} on the Fréchet conjunction/disjunction polytope (full derivations in App. C).

Empirically the bound holds on 100%100\% of the 1,8761{,}876 cliques. Mean bound-to-residual ratios are 1.301.30 (negation), 2.342.34 (disjunction), 3.003.00 (conjunction), and 4.394.39 (partition); the bound is tightest where the constraint normal aligns with the disagreement direction.

3.4 Quantitative magnitude prediction

Under uniform random owner-selection, the expected residual admits a closed form keyed to the empirical specialist covariance restricted to the constraint normal that defines the joint polytope. Let Π¯:=k−1​∑aΠa∈ℳ⋆\bar{\Pi}:=k^{-1}\sum_{a}\Pi_{a}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} (by convexity) and D:=diag⁡(ΣΠ)D:=\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma_{\Pi}) where ΣΠ:=k−1​∑a(Πa−Π¯)​(Πa−Π¯)⊤\Sigma_{\Pi}:=k^{-1}\sum_{a}(\Pi_{a}-\bar{\Pi})(\Pi_{a}-\bar{\Pi})^{\top}. Independent assignment across coordinates makes DD the effective covariance: 𝔼σ​[(x−Π¯)​(x−Π¯)⊤]=D\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(x-\bar{\Pi})(x-\bar{\Pi})^{\top}]=D.

Corollary 3.9 (Magnitude of ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}, Rayleigh-quotient form).

Suppose the joint polytope is locally defined by a single binding halfspace with normal aRa_{R} at the projection. Under uniform i.i.d. owner-selection,

𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]=κR⋅aR⊤​D​aR‖aR‖22,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\!\bigl[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}\bigr]\;=\;\kappa_{R}\cdot\frac{a_{R}^{\top}D\,a_{R}}{\|a_{R}\|_{2}^{2}}, (4)

where κR=1\kappa_{R}=1 when the binding constraint is an equality (aR⊤​Π¯=bRa_{R}^{\top}\bar{\Pi}=b_{R}). When the binding constraint is an inequality with Π¯\bar{\Pi} on the boundary, the law of aR⊤​(x−Π¯)a_{R}^{\top}(x-\bar{\Pi}) is the empirical distribution of {aR⊤​(Πa−Π¯)}a∈[k]\{a_{R}^{\top}(\Pi_{a}-\bar{\Pi})\}_{a\in[k]}; if this scalar is symmetric around 00 then κR=12\kappa_{R}=\tfrac{1}{2} exactly, and otherwise κR∈[0,1]\kappa_{R}\in[0,1] with κR≈12\kappa_{R}\approx\tfrac{1}{2} when the panel is approximately balanced about the boundary. The upper bound 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]≤aR⊤​D​aR/‖aR‖22\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}]\leq a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R}/\|a_{R}\|_{2}^{2} holds in all inequality cases, and the generic 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]≤tr⁡(D)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}]\leq\mathrm{tr}(D) holds without further assumptions. For the relation classes of Section 4: aneg=(1,1)a_{\textsc{neg}}=(1,1) (equality, κ=1\kappa=1); apartition=𝟏m⋆a_{\textsc{partition}}=\mathbf{1}_{m^{\star}} (equality, κ=1\kappa=1); aand,aora_{\textsc{and}},a_{\textsc{or}} are Fréchet halfspace normals (inequality, κ≈12\kappa\approx\tfrac{1}{2} under the symmetric-panel approximation; conjunction’s empirical κ≈0.83⋅12\kappa\!\approx\!0.83\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} reflects Π¯\bar{\Pi} off the boundary, see §5).

Proof sketch. Equality: ε⋆=|aR⊤​(x−Π¯)|/‖aR‖\varepsilon^{\star}=|a_{R}^{\top}(x-\bar{\Pi})|/\|a_{R}\|, square and use 𝔼σ​[aR⊤​(x−Π¯)​(x−Π¯)⊤​aR]=aR⊤​D​aR\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[a_{R}^{\top}(x-\bar{\Pi})(x-\bar{\Pi})^{\top}a_{R}]=a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R}. Inequality with Π¯\bar{\Pi} on the boundary: ε⋆=(aR⊤​(x−Π¯))+/‖aR‖\varepsilon^{\star}=(a_{R}^{\top}(x-\bar{\Pi}))_{+}/\|a_{R}\|; for a zero-mean random variable XX, 𝔼⁡[X+2]=12​𝔼​[X2]\mathbb{E}[X_{+}^{2}]=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[X^{2}] when XX is symmetric, otherwise 𝔼⁡[X+2]/𝔼⁡[X2]∈[0,1]\mathbb{E}[X_{+}^{2}]/\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]\in[0,1] depending on the upper-tail mass. Full proof and the generic-bound case in App. H.

Combined with Cor. 3.7, this yields a closed-form Brier tax 𝔼⁡[Brier⁡(r,y)−Brier⁡(Π⋆​(r),y)]≥κR​aR⊤​D​aR/‖aR‖2\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Brier}(r,y)-\mathrm{Brier}(\Pi^{\star}(r),y)]\geq\kappa_{R}\,a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R}/\|a_{R}\|^{2} when p⋆∈ℳ⋆p^{\star}\!\in\!\mathcal{M}^{\star}, computable from the panel covariance alone. The three couplings recurring in our experiments are shared-question disagreement (two specialists quote the same QQ at different prices), negation across components (pa+pb=1p_{a}\!+\!p_{b}\!=\!1), and partition across components (∑apa=1\sum_{a}p_{a}\!=\!1).

3.5 Hierarchical repair

The repair is constructive. Let Π𝒞:[0,1]m⋆→𝒞\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}:[0,1]^{m^{\star}}\to\mathcal{C} denote the L2L_{2} projection onto the coupling set, an intersection of finitely many half-spaces.

Theorem 3.10 (Hierarchical projection convergence).

Let {Π1,…,Πk,Π𝒞}\{\Pi_{1},\dots,\Pi_{k},\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}\} be the family of L2L_{2} projections onto the local polytopes {ℳa}\{\mathcal{M}_{a}\} (lifted to [0,1]m⋆[0,1]^{m^{\star}}) and the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Their intersection is the nonempty joint polytope ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}. The Boyle-Dykstra cyclic-projection iteration (Boyle and Dykstra, 1986) initialized at any r0∈[0,1]m⋆r_{0}\in[0,1]^{m^{\star}} generates a sequence converging in L2L_{2} to Π⋆​(r0)\Pi^{\star}(r_{0}).

Sketch.

ℳ⋆=(⋂aℳa↑)∩𝒞\mathcal{M}^{\star}=\bigl(\bigcap_{a}\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\uparrow}\bigr)\cap\mathcal{C} where ℳa↑\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\uparrow} is ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} lifted to [0,1]m⋆[0,1]^{m^{\star}} (free on non-component coordinates). Each Π∙\Pi_{\bullet} is the L2L_{2} projection onto a closed convex set, and each ℳa↑\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\uparrow} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is closed convex. By Bauschke and Combettes (2017, Thm. 9.31) (Boyle-Dykstra), cyclic L2L_{2} projection over a finite family of closed convex sets converges to the projection onto their intersection. ∎

Per-iteration cost.

Each Πa\Pi_{a} and Π𝒞\Pi_{\mathcal{C}} is a small QP. The Paleka (neg/and/or) and Polymarket (partition) relation classes admit closed-form projections (App. C); we use direct Π⋆\Pi^{\star} via OSQP (Stellato et al., 2020) for uniformity across relation classes, since the partition simplex projection and the negation closed form are mathematically equivalent to OSQP’s converged solution at the reported tolerance.

Where the cyclic machinery actually bites.

On the equality-coupled relations (negation, partition) the joint projection collapses to a single closed-form step (App. C): partition repair is simplex projection (Wang and Carreira-Perpiñán, 2013), which in the no-clipping majority is literally subtracting (∑ipi−1)/m⋆(\sum_{i}p_{i}\!-\!1)/m^{\star} from each coordinate. The Boyle–Dykstra cycle is mathematically equivalent to this but does real iterative work only on the Fréchet polytopes (conjunction, disjunction), where multiple half-spaces can be simultaneously active. The headline residual is therefore largest on the relation (partition) where the repair is simplest, and smallest where the cyclic machinery is needed; the contribution is operational, not algorithmic.

3.6 Runtime use

The residual supports three deployment modes that share the same computation and differ only in how the agent acts on it. In monitor mode the agent logs ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} and surfaces large residuals to an operator. In repair mode it replaces the naive composed quote with Π⋆​(⋅)\Pi^{\star}(\cdot) before passing it downstream. By Theorem 3.10 and Cor. 3.5, the repaired quote lies in ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} up to solver tolerance and the exposure diagnostic is driven to numerical zero. In abstain-or-escalate mode it refuses to act when ε⋆>τ\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!\tau, a risk–coverage knob whose calibration to budgeted exposure is outside our scope.

3.7 Sequential monitoring: anytime-valid coherence test

In long-horizon agent deployments the agent generates a compositional residual stream (εt⋆)t≥1(\varepsilon^{\star}_{t})_{t\geq 1} across successive composition steps. The spatial guarantee of Section 3 certifies incoherence at each step; the following temporal guarantee lets an operator certify persistent incoherence across the stream without fixing a stopping horizon in advance.

Under the null H0H_{0} that the composed population quote is jointly coherent (pF⋆∈ℳ⋆p_{F}^{\star}\!\in\!\mathcal{M}^{\star} at each step), the e-process Et​(λ):=∏s=1texp⁡(λ⁡(εs⋆2−ms⋆/(4​Ks))−λ2​ms⋆/(2​Ks))E_{t}(\lambda):=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\exp\!\bigl(\lambda(\varepsilon_{s}^{\star 2}-m_{s}^{\star}/(4K_{s}))-\lambda^{2}m_{s}^{\star}/(2K_{s})\bigr) is a non-negative ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-supermartingale (Lemma D.1, App. D). By Ville’s inequality (Ville, 1939; Howard et al., 2021), the stopping rule τα:=inf{t:Et​(λ)≥1/α}\tau_{\alpha}:=\inf\{t:E_{t}(\lambda)\geq 1/\alpha\} controls Type-I error at level α\alpha uniformly over all stopping times (Theorem D.2). An operator monitors EtE_{t} online and escalates the agent pipeline when it crosses 1/α1/\alpha; no fixed-horizon commitment is required. The full derivation and empirical demonstration on four LLM residual streams appear in Appendix D.

4 Experimental setup

We evaluate on Paleka (Paleka et al., 2025) (negation, conjunction, disjunction, paraphrase; 134134 cliques per checker) and Polymarket (6767 partition cliques after leakage control, expanded to 268268 ensemble instances by four seeds). Both benchmarks were chosen because they target the regime the theory predicts will be tightest: Paleka was constructed by Paleka et al. (2025) for cross-question consistency checking, and Polymarket’s partition events are the unit-mass constraint regime (∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1) where the polytope coupling is most restrictive.

Models.

Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 (via the Anthropic Messages API), OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano (via Azure OpenAI), and Meta llama-3.3-70b-versatile (via Groq). Frontier-panel evaluations additionally use OpenAI gpt-5.5 (via Azure OpenAI). These are the public API model identifiers as returned by each provider on 30 April 2026; raw responses, prompts, and per-clique residuals are released with the supplementary material. Each specialist produces K=8K{=}8 verbalized probability samples per question at temperature 0.70.7.

Leakage control.

Polymarket events were filtered so that every market in every retained event resolved strictly after our model snapshot date of 30 April 2026; the inclusion cutoff was 1 May 2026, and all retained events resolved on or after that date. Paleka cliques inherit the resolution-status verification of Paleka et al. (2025). Full filtering protocol in Appendix E.

Scope of the evaluation.

The bulk of our evaluation is a controlled routing simulation: clique coordinates are assigned i.i.d. to specialists from the panel, and the composed quote is reassembled by owner-selected aggregation. The planner-discretion harness (§5.3) and routing-protocol ladder (App. O) are the closest stand-ins for a deployed multi-component agent; both are small (n=20n\!=\!20 and n=100n\!=\!100 partitions respectively). Claims about end-to-end deployed agents should be read with that scope in mind.

Compositional ensemble.

For each clique with mm questions, we draw 44 random seeds; each seed assigns each of the mm questions to one of the 44 LLMs uniformly i.i.d.; the agent’s quoted marginal on coordinate jj is the JCD-projected marginal of the assigned LLM on that coordinate. The source forecast from each LLM is JCD-coherent on the full clique before coordinate selection; the ensemble residual ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} therefore reflects exclusively cross-component disagreement.

Benchmark properties.

The four relation classes admit closed-form local projections (App. C) and span a range of polytope geometries from a single equality (negation), to a high-dimensional simplex (partition), to the Fréchet box (and/or). The coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} controls the gap between ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} and ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, and random vs. structured routing brackets cross-model mixing. Theorem 3.3’s prediction ε⋆≡0\varepsilon^{\star}\!\equiv\!0 when ℳ⋆=ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}\!=\!\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes} is verified at the QP solver floor by the no-composition reference (Figure 2b, gray dashed), a falsifiable test of the dichotomy.

5 Results

The random-assignment experiment (N=134N\!=\!134 cliques × 4\times\,4 seeds =536=\!536 per relation for Paleka, plus N=×=268N\!=\!67\!\times\!4\!=\!268 for Polymarket; total 1,8761{,}876) and structured-routing variant (N=469N\!=\!469, one deterministic seed) bracket cross-model mixing.

5.1 Compositional residual and controls

Compositional residual under random routing.

The compositional residual is strictly positive on 94%94\% (partition), 66%66\% (negation), 43%43\% (disjunction), 33%33\% (conjunction) of cliques (Figure 2a). Mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} ranges 0.0580.058 (and) to 0.1180.118 (partition) on the full N=1,876N\!=\!1{,}876 ensemble. The projection-step ablation (App. I, Table I) reports 0.054/0.0980.054/0.098 on the same relations because it is restricted to the resolved-label subset on which paired Brier is computed (∼85%\sim\!85\% of the ensemble); the ∼20%\sim\!20\% magnitude shift on partition reflects that unresolved partition cliques tend to be larger-m⋆m^{\star} events with proportionally higher residuals. None is visible per-component, where each Πa∈ℳa\Pi_{a}\!\in\!\mathcal{M}_{a} has zero residual. Hierarchical JCD reduces the mean exposure bound m⋆​ε⋆\sqrt{m^{\star}}\varepsilon^{\star} to ×10−141.7\!\times\!10^{-14} on the 1,8761{,}876-clique ensemble (per-clique post-repair ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} reaches the OSQP primal-residual floor of ≤×10−16\leq\!1.5\!\times\!10^{-16} on partition and negation, where closed-form projections terminate at machine precision; the ensemble mean is dominated by the and/or relations, which bottom out at the iterative-OSQP tolerance instead), matching the no-composition reference (a single LLM on every coordinate; Figure 2b, gray) while retaining specialist routing.

Empirical validation of the magnitude prediction.

Cor. 3.9’s Rayleigh-quotient prediction κR​aR⊤​D​aR/‖aR‖2\kappa_{R}\,a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R}/\|a_{R}\|^{2} matches the observed expected residual 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}] across all four relation classes (Table 1; per-clique Pearson 0.690.69–0.890.89). The conjunction under-shoot reflects Π¯\bar{\Pi} typically interior to the binding Fréchet halfspace; on the remaining three relations the prediction is tight to within 7%7\%. Both ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} and the m⋆​ε⋆\sqrt{m^{\star}}\varepsilon^{\star} exposure bound are therefore predictable from the panel covariance alone, before any routing.

Same-model decoupling control.

To separate coordinate isolation from cross-model capability divergence, we re-ran with four fresh-seed runs of one model (Claude-Haiku-4.5, N=80N{=}80 cliques per relation, 4040 partitions). Mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} falls to 0.025/0.019/0.040/0.0580.025/0.019/0.040/0.058 on neg/and/or/partition: 2222–60%60\% of the residual persists at same-model, with cross-model heterogeneity amplifying by 1.71.7–4.5×4.5\times. A greedy-decoding (T=0T{=}0) control retains ε⋆=0.025\varepsilon^{\star}=0.025–0.0960.096 across relations (App. J); on negation and disjunction T=0T{=}0 amplifies the residual relative to T=0.7T{=}0.7, ruling out sampling noise as the source.

Compositional Brier against resolved labels.

We adopt the convention Δ​Brier=BrierJCD−Briernaive\Delta\mathrm{Brier}=\mathrm{Brier}_{\mathrm{JCD}}-\mathrm{Brier}_{\mathrm{naive}} throughout, so a negative Δ\Delta indicates JCD improvement. Paired over the 1,8761{,}876 cliques, hierarchical JCD reduces compositional Brier on Neg (Δ​Brier=−0.0137\Delta\mathrm{Brier}{=}-0.0137, p<10−43p{<}10^{-43}), And (Δ​Brier=−0.0076\Delta\mathrm{Brier}{=}-0.0076, p<10−16p{<}10^{-16}), and Partition (Δ​Brier=−0.0048\Delta\mathrm{Brier}{=}-0.0048, p<10−23p{<}10^{-23}). Or is marginal (Δ​Brier=+0.0027\Delta\mathrm{Brier}{=}{+}0.0027, p=0.07p{=}0.07): this is the predicted reversal regime of Cor. 3.7, where label noise on a small fraction of disjunction resolutions pushes p⋆p^{\star} outside ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}, and Cor. 3.7’s condition-and-reversal allows projection to amplify error there rather than reduce it.

Disagreement-driven mechanism.

Per-clique ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} regressed on the assignment-aware reference disagreement minβ⁡‖x−Πβ‖2\min_{\beta}\|x{-}\Pi_{\beta}\|_{2} (Prop. 3.8) gives R2=0.93R^{2}{=}0.93 on negation (slope 0.830.83) and R2=0.58R^{2}{=}0.58–0.640.64 on and/or/partition (slope 0.590.59–0.630.63). The constraint normal aligns most closely with the disagreement direction on negation; on higher-dimensional polytopes the projection contracts components of disagreement orthogonal to the binding halfspace, loosening the bound.

Robustness to routing topology and retrieval grounding.

Under structured routing (one model per relation family; App. L), ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 98.5%98.5\% of negation, 36%36\% partition, 16%16\% disjunction, 12%12\% conjunction cliques; mean m⋆​ε⋆=0.117\sqrt{m^{\star}}\varepsilon^{\star}\!=\!0.117 vs. 0.1370.137 under random routing. Retrieval grounding (top-55 DuckDuckGo snippets per specialist) on 3030 partitions shifts mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} from 0.2600.260 to 0.2830.283; 20/3020/30 partitions are equal-or-worse with retrieval (App. P).

Routing-protocol ladder.

On 100100 multi-candidate partitions (App. O) we walk the routing protocol from fixed naive owner-selection to autonomous tool-using planners. Prompt-engineering under owner-selection drops mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} from 0.2350.235 (isolated) to 0.0900.090 (listed) to 0.0810.081 (full); isolated →\to listed is significant (p<10−11p\!<\!10^{-11}), listed →\to full is not (p=0.18p\!=\!0.18), and 99%99\% of partitions retain ε⋆>10−3\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!10^{-3} under full. Tool-using planners with delegate-and-submit tools further reduce ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}: a non-reasoning planner reaches ε⋆=0.009/0.004\varepsilon^{\star}\!=\!0.009/0.004 at ∼×m\sim\!4.8\!\times m calls; a frontier reasoning planner reaches 0/2000/200 positive residuals at ∼×m\sim\!6.7\!\times m calls. The hierarchical projection reaches ε⋆→0\varepsilon^{\star}\!\to\!0 at ×m1\!\times m specialist calls (Theorem 3.10).

5.2 Intuitive LLM-side mitigations fail

The retrieval-grounding and routing-ladder results above each isolate one obvious LLM-side fix. We collect them with a third candidate, delegating coherentisation to an aggregator LLM, and compare all three to the geometric repair. The comparison is deliberately stacked in favour of the geometric repair: the projection is handed the explicit coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a typed input, while the three prompt-based methods have to infer it from natural-language context. The genuinely hard regime where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is implicit in free-form planner-tool transcripts is outside the scope of all four interventions here and is discussed as future work (§6). Table 2 reports mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}, the fraction of partitions retaining ε⋆>0.05\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0.05, and the fraction regressing relative to naive composition. Retrieval grounding regresses on 20/3020/30 partitions: mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} rises from 0.2600.260 to 0.2830.283 on the matched 3030-partition baseline. (Table 2’s “Naive” row reports 0.2140.214, the 100100-partition mean used for the LLM-aggregator comparison; the two subsets are flagged in the caption.) Partition-aware prompting helps on average (0.0660.066) but 53%53\% of partitions still exceed the 0.050.05 band and 5/305/30 regress. LLM-as-aggregator reduces mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} to 0.0280.028 but 15%15\% of partitions still exceed 0.050.05 and 7/1007/100 regress against the naive baseline. The geometric repair eliminates the residual to the QP solver floor (≤×10−16\leq 1.5\!\times\!10^{-16}) at 11ms per partition with no extra LLM call. Prompt-only and aggregator-LLM mitigations can harm already-coherent quotes: across both prompt-side interventions, 9/109/10 worsening cases had baseline ε⋆<0.05\varepsilon^{\star}\!<\!0.05, so ε⋆>τ\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!\tau also serves as a gate for when these prompt-based repairs are safe to apply.

5.3 Planner-discretion harness

To check that the failure is not an artefact of random assignment, we re-run the experiment with a planner LLM (Claude-Haiku-4.5) that, for each of 2020 live-style partitions, picks a specialist per outcome from the four-LLM roster and emits its own per-specialist context block; specialists then sample K=8K{=}8 verbalized probabilities under the planner’s prompt and we compute ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} as in §4. Mean ε⋆=0.113\varepsilon^{\star}=0.113 versus 0.2310.231 under random assignment on the same partitions (15/2015/20 improve), but ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 20/2020/20. The planner’s routing histogram (GPT-5.4-mini 50%50\%, Claude-Haiku 31%31\%, Llama-70b 13%13\%, GPT-nano 6%6\%) shows no self-routing.

5.4 Mechanism probe: coupling-visible elicitation

The mechanism claim of §3 is that ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} arises because specialists do not see the coupling constraint. We test this directly. On the same 2020 partitions of §5.3, we re-elicit each specialist’s quote under two paired conditions. Blind keeps the planner-chosen routing of §5.3 but strips the planner-emitted context, so the specialist sees only its assigned outcome as a single Bernoulli question. Informed keeps the same routing and additionally shows the specialist the partition label, all sibling outcomes, the explicit ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}\!=\!1 constraint, and the peers’ Blind quotes on the other outcomes. Each (partition, condition) cell is replicated across four independent K=8K\!=\!8 sampling rounds, paired Blind→\toInformed within each round. Informed varies two things at once (coupling visibility and peer-quote disclosure), so the comparison identifies coupling-visible elicitation with peer context as the intervention, not constraint visibility in isolation; full setup in App. S.

Disclosing the coupling constraint (and peer quotes) reduces ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} as the theory predicts: paired mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} falls from 0.5190.519 Blind to 0.2980.298 Informed on 16/2016/20 partitions, with 11 unchanged and 33 worsened. The Blind mean of 0.5190.519 exceeds both the random-assignment mean (0.2310.231) and the planner-harness mean (0.1130.113) on these same 2020 partitions. Two protocol differences combine: the planner harness lets a planner LLM see the partition when choosing routing (and emit its own per-specialist context), while Blind strips all such context; and the four Blind seeds are independent K=8K\!=\!8 sampling rounds on the same planner-chosen routing, so cross-seed variance does not average out as it does over random reshuffles. We did not isolate the contributions further; the residual gap is observed, not theory-derived. The three worsening partitions are non-payoff multi-way forecasts where Blind specialists were already roughly normalised; per-partition detail in App. S. The intervention is partial, not a fix: ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} remains positive on every Informed partition, consistent with the LLM-side mitigations result (§5.2) that no purely prompt-based intervention eliminates the residual. The geometric repair remains the only intervention that drives ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} to the QP floor on every partition.

5.5 Frontier-panel rerun

To test whether capability scaling closes the gap, we rerun the random-assignment ensemble on the 6767 Polymarket partition cliques with a frontier-only specialist roster: Claude-Opus-4.7, GPT-5.5 (reasoning disabled for apples-to-apples), DeepSeek-V3.2, and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E (FP8). The protocol matches §4 exactly (K=8K{=}8, simplex pre-projection, 44 seeds, 268268 ensemble bets). The residual persists: ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 97.8%97.8\% of the 268268 clique-seed bets, slightly above the mid-tier panel’s 94%94\% on the same Polymarket slice. Mean ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} drops from 0.1180.118 to 0.0720.072 (−39%-39\%): frontier models reduce residual magnitude on partitions but do not eliminate the failure mode. Brier improvement under hierarchical JCD remains highly significant (Δ​Brier=−0.012\Delta\mathrm{Brier}=-0.012, 95%95\% paired-bootstrap CI [−0.015,−0.009][-0.015,-0.009]); the log-payoff gain trends positive (+0.107+0.107 nats per bet) but is noisier on this narrower slice. Table 4 reports the full frontier-vs-mid-tier comparison.

5.6 Downstream-decision regret

For each of 1,7701{,}770 resolved ensemble bets from §4 (we drop 106/1,876106/1{,}876 where the assigned specialist lacks a forecast for the assigned coordinate, a pipeline artefact on partition events) we convert the composed quote p^⋆\hat{p}^{\star} into a proportional allocation wi=max⁡(p^i⋆,0)/∑jmax⁡(p^j⋆,0)w_{i}=\max(\hat{p}^{\star}_{i},0)/\sum_{j}\max(\hat{p}^{\star}_{j},0) and measure (i) Brier loss against the binary resolution vector and (ii) the realised log-payoff log⁡wwinner\log w_{\text{winner}} on the 1,2521{,}252 bets with a unique YES. The proportional rule passes the agent’s incoherent quote through to the bettor’s allocation, which exposes the behavioural cost of compositional incoherence in its rawest form; stricter rules (truncated Kelly, max-entropy) that themselves coherentise the quote partially absorb this cost into the bettor’s strategy, so their log-payoff gains under JCD are correspondingly smaller (Table 6).

Hierarchical JCD lowers mean Brier (Δ​Brier=−0.018\Delta\mathrm{Brier}=-0.018, paired-bootstrap 95%95\% CI over (clique, seed): [−0.021,−0.015][-0.021,-0.015]) and improves mean log-payoff by +0.115+0.115 nats per bet ([+0.056,+0.187][+0.056,+0.187]). JCD matches the single-LLM oracle’s gain (Δ​Brier=−0.017\Delta\mathrm{Brier}=-0.017, CI [−0.035,−0.000][-0.035,-0.000]) with a confidence interval ∼6×\sim\!6\times narrower. The effect concentrates on partitions (naive loses 0.600.60 nats/bet vs. JCD, CI [+0.15,+1.15][+0.15,+1.15], n=162n{=}162). The Pythagorean Brier improvement of Cor. 3.6 is thus realised on resolved labels, not only on the synthetic ε⋆2\varepsilon^{\star 2} slack.

Regret stratifies by certificate.

The realised regret rises monotonically with ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} (Table 5): the bottom two quartiles (where ε⋆≤0.004\varepsilon^{\star}\!\leq\!0.004) carry no measurable Brier or log-payoff gain, while the top quartile (where ε⋆>0.154\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0.154) accounts for 0.0540.054 Brier and 0.2210.221 nats of regret per bet. This justifies the runtime-gating recipe of §5.7: applying the projection only when ε⋆>τ\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!\tau targets precisely the high-regret bets.

Allocation-rule sensitivity.

The log-payoff gain depends on how a downstream bettor allocates on top of the agent’s quote. Brier is allocation-rule independent (−0.018-0.018 across all rules). Under the proportional rule (the agent’s incoherence is passed through as allocation slack), JCD beats naive by +0.168+0.168 nats/bet on the 1,2521{,}252 unique-YES subset (95%95\% CI [+0.083,+0.263][+0.083,+0.263]); the +0.115+0.115 figure cited in the abstract is the same comparison averaged over the full 1,7701{,}770-bet ensemble (non-unique-YES bets contribute zero log-payoff). Under stricter rules that themselves coherentise the quote (truncated Kelly, max-entropy), the gain shrinks to +0.006+0.006 nats: the bettor has already absorbed the agent’s incoherence into its own strategy (Table 6).

5.7 Runtime gating thresholds

The deployment recommendation is to apply repair (or escalate) only when ε⋆>τ\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!\tau. We calibrate τ\tau on the 1,770-bet ensemble of §5.6, treating top-quartile log-payoff regret as the harm signal. Brier-regret is mechanically tied to ε⋆2\varepsilon^{\star 2} by Cor. 3.6; log-payoff regret depends on which coordinate resolved YES and is therefore not geometrically tied to ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}, making it the genuinely informative discrimination test.

Discrimination.

ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} predicts top-quartile log-payoff regret with 55-fold cross-validated AUC ±0.0440.775\!\pm\!0.044; the geometric Brier-regret check gives CV-AUC ±0.0120.974\!\pm\!0.012. Mean realised log-payoff regret stratifies cleanly by ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} quartile (0.000,0.000,0.123,0.2210.000,0.000,0.123,0.221 nats, bottom to top; Table 5).

Operating thresholds.

A high-recall threshold τ=0.15\tau\!=\!0.15 catches 91%91\% of harmful bets at a 25%25\% alert rate and 3%3\% false-alarm rate; a high-precision threshold τ=0.22\tau\!=\!0.22 catches 51%51\% at 14%14\% alert rate and 1.5%1.5\% FPR (Table 7). Both thresholds are stable under 55-fold CV (at τ=0.15\tau\!=\!0.15: mean alert rate 25%25\%, mean recall 90%90\%). For deployment we recommend τ≈0.15\tau\!\approx\!0.15 when repair is cheap and τ≈0.22\tau\!\approx\!0.22 when escalation is costly.

5.8 Per-component layer (summary)

The local JCD layer behaves as Theorem A.1 predicts. Sorting Paleka cliques by pre-projection ε\varepsilon, JCD’s Brier gain stratifies to the most-incoherent quartile (0.0400.040 at m=2m{=}2, 0.0130.013 at m=3m{=}3; 0.120.12 on Polymarket at m≥4m{\geq}4); other quartiles show no detectable gain (Figure 4). Stacked with per-question Platt calibration (Platt, 1999) (baseline B6 of App. G), JCD reduces mean Brier on every (model,checker)(\text{model},\text{checker}) cell, by 0.0370.037 on Paleka and 0.0460.046 on Polymarket; Diebold–Mariano p<10−4p<10^{-4} on every model. A Murphy decomposition (Table 13) attributes the gain to calibration (36%36\% reliability reduction) rather than over-extremization. Per-relation B6 gains on Paleka (−21%-21\% and, −37%-37\% or, −4%-4\% neg, −1%-1\% paraphrase) track local-polytope restrictiveness.

Reproducibility.

Code, prompts, sample dumps, per-clique JCD residuals, the ensemble-assignment seed, and the full hierarchical-projection pipeline are documented in Appendix E and released at https://github.com/akotawala10/composition-incoherence-icml; KK-sweep and the sequential test appear in Appendix D.

6 Conclusion

The compositional residual ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} supplies the instance-wise, distribution-free coherence guarantee that per-component calibration, self-consistency, and conformal prediction do not: it is computable at deployment from system output and the cross-component constraints alone, certifies a Dutch-book exposure no per-component repair can remove, and admits a deterministic projection-based fix. The product-structure dichotomy (Theorem 3.3) characterises when local coherence implies global coherence; Cor. 3.9 predicts the typical residual from the panel covariance, matching observed 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}] within 7%7\% on three of four relation classes; the hierarchical Boyle–Dykstra projection eliminates ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} at ×m1\!\times\!m elicitation cost; and on 1,7701{,}770 resolved bets the certificate yields +0.115+0.115 nats per bet over naive composition. The guarantees are orthogonal to per-output conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021) and complementary to opinion pooling (Genest and Zidek, 1986; Abbas, 2009), which requires every expert to forecast every coordinate.

Limitations.

The Rayleigh-quotient prediction of Cor. 3.9 is exact for negation and partition cliques but conservative when the panel mean Π¯\bar{\Pi} lies in the interior of the binding Fréchet halfspace, which produces the ×0.83\!\times under-shoot we observe on conjunction.

The principal scope condition is that the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is specified explicitly: every theorem in §3 treats 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a finite, externally given list of half-spaces and equalities over joint coordinates (shared-question identifications, cross-component logical relations, partition-mass constraints). This covers structured tool-use and function-calling deployments, where the planner emits declared output schemas with typed sub-question fields and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is recoverable from the schema without language understanding. Our planner-discretion harness (§4) and routing-protocol ladder (App. O) target this regime.

It does not cover deployments in which 𝒞\mathcal{C} is implicit in free-form chain-of-thought or in unstructured planner–tool transcripts. There, ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} remains well-defined and the Boyle–Dykstra repair still applies on any subsequently specified polytope, but the certificate cannot be computed without first recovering 𝒞\mathcal{C} from the trace. Partial routes to that recovery exist as components: an NLI-style classifier over sub-question pairs, schema-enforcing planner protocols, and symbolic trace logging at the tool-call boundary. A unified inference step remains open; we list it as the first future-work item below.

Finally, our resolved-label experiment relies on Polymarket resolutions, which are noisy on a small fraction of disjunction cliques; this pushes p⋆p^{\star} outside ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} on those cliques and is the regime where Cor. 3.7 does not guarantee improvement.

Future work.

First, the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is currently provided externally; recovering 𝒞\mathcal{C} from unstructured planner–tool traces would extend ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} to free-form agent transcripts, where the cross-component constraints are implicit in the prompt structure rather than typed. Second, the L2L_{2}/Brier pairing is one instance of a broader matched-Bregman recipe; substituting log-loss or spherical scoring rules yields analogous projections under their respective Bregman geometries (Banerjee et al., 2005), with the residual generalising to a Bregman gap. Third, the spatial certificate of Theorem 3.3 and the temporal e-process of §3.7 compose step-by-step but ignore long-horizon dependence between steps; a sequential certificate that exploits inter-step structure is open.

Broader Impact

A runtime certificate for system-level coherence can be wired into deployed multi-component pipelines as a guardrail, surfacing incoherent compositions before they reach a downstream decision policy. This is a reliability and auditability gain for high-stakes settings such as forecasting, decision support, and regulated probabilistic reasoning. The corresponding risk is over-trust: a small ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} certifies coherence of the quoted belief but says nothing about whether the underlying specialists are calibrated against the true distribution, and a projected quote may be confidently wrong on the very inputs where its components disagree most. Operators deploying the repair should therefore report ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} alongside conventional calibration and coverage diagnostics, not as a substitute for them.

Appendix A Within-component projection facts

Theorem A.1 (Pythagorean Brier improvement).

Let p∗∈ℳCp^{*}\!\in\!\mathcal{M}_{C} be the ground-truth marginal for clique CC and Π⁡(p^)\Pi(\hat{p}) the L2L_{2} projection of p^\hat{p} onto ℳC\mathcal{M}_{C}. Then for any p^∈ℝm\hat{p}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{m}, ‖Π⁡(p^)−p∗‖22≤‖p^−p∗‖22−‖p^−Π⁡(p^)‖22\|\Pi(\hat{p})-p^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\hat{p}-p^{*}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\hat{p}-\Pi(\hat{p})\|_{2}^{2}. The slack ‖p^−Π⁡(p^)‖22\|\hat{p}-\Pi(\hat{p})\|_{2}^{2} is the squared distance from coherence; Brier improvement is largest where pre-projection incoherence is largest.

Proof.

Hilbert projection theorem (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017, Thm. 3.16) gives ⟨p^−Π⁡(p^),p∗−Π⁡(p^)⟩≤0\langle\hat{p}-\Pi(\hat{p}),\,p^{*}-\Pi(\hat{p})\rangle\leq 0. Expand ‖p^−p∗‖2\|\hat{p}-p^{*}\|^{2} around Π⁡(p^)\Pi(\hat{p}) and drop the non-negative cross term. ∎

Corollary A.2 (Per-component finite-state FTAP).

Treating Π⁡(p^)∈ℳC\Pi(\hat{p})\!\in\!\mathcal{M}_{C} as quoted unit-pay prices on the mm Bernoulli contracts of CC, the finite-state Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing rules out a state-independent Dutch book against the ideal projection. Under a numerical QP solution the unit-stake exposure diagnostic is bounded by m⋅εKKT≤×10−5m\cdot\varepsilon^{\mathrm{KKT}}\!\leq\!1.4\!\times\!10^{-5} at OSQP default tolerance.

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 3.3 (reverse direction)

Suppose ℳ⋆⊊ℳ⊠\mathcal{M}^{\star}\subsetneq\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}. Pick any r∈ℳ⊠∖ℳ⋆r\in\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}\setminus\mathcal{M}^{\star}. For each component aa, set p^(a)\hat{p}^{(a)} to the restriction of rr to component aa’s coordinates: p^i(a):=rj⁡(a,i)\hat{p}^{(a)}_{i}:=r_{j(a,i)} where j⁡(a,i)j(a,i) is the joint index that component aa’s ii-th local coordinate maps to under Definition 3.2; under shared-question coupling, set p^ia(a)=p^ib(b)=rj\hat{p}^{(a)}_{i_{a}}=\hat{p}^{(b)}_{i_{b}}=r_{j} whenever components aa and bb both own the duplicate of joint coordinate jj. Then each restriction lies in ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} since r∈ℳ⊠r\in\mathcal{M}^{\boxtimes}, so Πa​(p^(a))\Pi_{a}(\hat{p}^{(a)}) equals that restriction and the owner-selected aggregator reassembles 𝒜⁡(Π1,…,Πk)=r\mathcal{A}(\Pi_{1},\dots,\Pi_{k})=r. Since r∉ℳ⋆r\notin\mathcal{M}^{\star} and ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} is closed, Π⋆​(r)≠r\Pi^{\star}(r)\neq r and ε⋆=‖r−Π⋆​(r)‖2>0\varepsilon^{\star}=\|r-\Pi^{\star}(r)\|_{2}>0.

Appendix D Sequential test on the residual stream

In long-horizon agent deployments, the compositional residual stream (εt⋆)t≥1(\varepsilon^{\star}_{t})_{t\geq 1} can be monitored over time; the per-component test below extends to the system level once a bounded-difference envelope for the chosen aggregation rule is specified. Under coordinate-selection aggregation with disjoint owners, εt⋆2\varepsilon_{t}^{\star 2} inherits the envelope below with mtm_{t} replaced by mt⋆m^{\star}_{t} and KtK_{t} replaced by mina⁡Ka,t\min_{a}K_{a,t}. The compositional theory of Section 3 is spatial: it controls coherence at a single time step across kk components. The residual stream (εt)t≥1(\varepsilon_{t})_{t\geq 1} that an agent generates over time admits a complementary temporal guarantee.

Setup.

A clique stream (Ct)t≥1(C_{t})_{t\geq 1} with sizes mtm_{t} and KtK_{t} samples per question yields residuals εt=‖p^t−Π⁡(p^t)‖2\varepsilon_{t}=\|\hat{p}_{t}-\Pi(\hat{p}_{t})\|_{2}. Assume the Kt​mtK_{t}m_{t} samples at time tt are conditionally independent given ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, each bounded in [0,1][0,1] (Bernoulli parses or verbalized-probability emissions both satisfy this; the bounded-difference constant below uses the worst-case [0,1][0,1] variance 1/41/4, which majorises the verbalized-sample variance), with conditional mean vector pF(t)p_{F}^{(t)}. Define the null H0:pF(t)∈ℳC(t)​for all t.H_{0}:\,p_{F}^{(t)}\in\mathcal{M}_{C}^{(t)}\ \text{for all $t$}.

Lemma D.1 (Bounded-difference MGF bound).

Under H0H_{0}, εt2∈[0,mt]\varepsilon_{t}^{2}\in[0,m_{t}] with conditional mean 𝔼⁡[εt2∣ℱt−1]≤mt/(4​Kt)\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq m_{t}/(4K_{t}), and for every λ>0\lambda>0, 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ⁡(εt2−mt/(4​Kt)))∣ℱt−1]≤exp⁡(λ2​mt/(2​Kt)).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\bigl(\lambda(\varepsilon_{t}^{2}-m_{t}/(4K_{t}))\bigr)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\leq\exp\!\bigl(\lambda^{2}m_{t}/(2K_{t})\bigr).

Proof.

εt≤‖p^t−pF(t)‖2\varepsilon_{t}\leq\|\hat{p}_{t}-p_{F}^{(t)}\|_{2} under H0H_{0} by projection optimality on ℳC\mathcal{M}_{C}. The squared norm Zt=‖p^t−pF(t)‖22Z_{t}=\|\hat{p}_{t}-p_{F}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2} is a function of Kt​mtK_{t}m_{t} i.i.d. [0,1][0,1]-bounded samples with bounded differences 2/Kt2/K_{t} per sample; McDiarmid’s bounded-difference inequality (McDiarmid, 1989) yields the sub-Gaussian MGF bound 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ⁡(Zt−𝔼​Zt))]≤exp⁡(λ2​mt/(2​Kt))\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(Z_{t}-\mathbb{E}Z_{t}))]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}m_{t}/(2K_{t})), and 𝔼​Zt≤mt/(4​Kt)\mathbb{E}Z_{t}\leq m_{t}/(4K_{t}) from the per-component variance bound. ∎

Theorem D.2 (Anytime-valid coherence test).

For any λ>0\lambda>0, Et​(λ):=∏s=1texp⁡(λ⁡(εs2−ms/(4​Ks))−λ2​ms/(2​Ks)),E0=1,E_{t}(\lambda):=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\exp(\lambda(\varepsilon_{s}^{2}-m_{s}/(4K_{s}))-\lambda^{2}m_{s}/(2K_{s})),\ E_{0}=1, is a non-negative ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-supermartingale under H0H_{0}. Hence by Ville’s inequality (Ville, 1939; Howard et al., 2021), for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and every stopping time τ\tau, ℙ⁡(supt≤τEt​(λ)≥1/α∣H0)≤α.\mathbb{P}\bigl(\sup_{t\leq\tau}E_{t}(\lambda)\geq 1/\alpha\mid H_{0}\bigr)\leq\alpha. The decision rule τα:=inf{t:Et≥1/α}\tau_{\alpha}:=\inf\{t:E_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\} controls Type-I error at level α\alpha uniformly over stopping rules.

Proof.

Each factor of Et​(λ)E_{t}(\lambda) is non-negative. By Lemma D.1, 𝔼[Et/Et−1∣ℱt−1]≤exp(λ2mt/(2Kt))exp(−λ2mt/(2Kt))=1\mathbb{E}[E_{t}/E_{t-1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}m_{t}/(2K_{t}))\exp(-\lambda^{2}m_{t}/(2K_{t}))=1, the supermartingale property. Ville’s inequality yields the maximal bound, uniform over stopping times by optional stopping. ∎

Tuning λ\lambda.

For the alternative 𝔼⁡[εt2]→mt/(4​Kt)+δ\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t}^{2}]\to m_{t}/(4K_{t})+\delta, the bounded-difference-optimal bet is λ∗=δ​Kt/mt\lambda^{*}=\delta K_{t}/m_{t}; we mix over a log grid λ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1,2,5,10}\lambda\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1,2,5,10\} in our experiments (Figure 3), retaining anytime-valid coverage by linearity (Ramdas et al., 2023).

Empirical demonstration.

Figure 3 runs the test on each model’s per-clique residual stream (N=603N{=}603 cliques per model, fixed-seed shuffle). Three of four models reject H0H_{0} at α≤10−4\alpha\leq 10^{-4} within ≤422\leq\!422 cliques (Llama-3.3-70b at t=16t=16, GPT-5.4-nano at t=177t=177, GPT-5.4-mini at t=422t=422); Claude-Haiku-4.5 has mean residual below the H0H_{0}-envelope at K=8K{=}8 and is not rejected within 603603 cliques, demonstrating that the test calibrates power against the bounded-difference envelope. The same construction applies to the compositional residual stream (εt⋆)(\varepsilon^{\star}_{t}) from Section 3 after replacing the per-component envelope by the corresponding envelope for the agent’s aggregation rule.

Appendix E Clique-mining pipeline and reproducibility

Paleka.

Tuples are pre-mined by the original authors: each JSONL record is a single (checker,{Qi},relation)(\mathrm{checker},\{Q_{i}\},\mathrm{relation}) entry, parsed directly.

Polymarket.

We query gamma-api at the event level, retain events with ≥2\geq\!2 resolved markets, and emit one of two relation types: (i) a partition relation ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1 when an event has multi-candidate markets that resolve with exactly one YES (e.g. election winners, sports brackets); (ii) an implication ladder when an event has multiple threshold markets “X above kk” at ascending kk. Events are capped at m≤8m{\leq}8 markets.

Compositional ensemble.

For each clique with mm questions and 44 LLMs, we draw 44 random seeds (independent across cliques and seeds, fixed master seed) and for each seed assign each question jj to one of the 44 LLMs uniformly; the agent’s quoted marginal on coordinate jj is the jj-th coordinate of the assigned LLM’s JCD-projected forecast. Hierarchical JCD applies Π⋆\Pi^{\star} to the resulting concatenated vector (in our experiments equal to direct JCD on the joint clique, which by Theorem 3.10 is the converged Dykstra projection through the local-then-coupling cycle).

Leakage control.

Every Polymarket event in the evaluation slice resolved after the latest model snapshot (30 April 2026). Paleka cliques inherit Paleka et al. (2025)’s own resolution-status verification.

Reproducibility manifest.

Table 8 records the exact configuration used to produce every number in the paper. The released artifact (https://github.com/akotawala10/composition-incoherence-icml) contains the sample dumps, per-clique JCD residuals, ensemble-assignment seeds, and the hierarchical-projection pipeline.

Appendix H Proof of Cor. 3.9 (Rayleigh-quotient magnitude bound)

We give the proof under uniform i.i.d. owner-selection σ:[m⋆]→[k]\sigma:[m^{\star}]\!\to\![k], with Π¯:=k−1​∑aΠa\bar{\Pi}:=k^{-1}\sum_{a}\Pi_{a} and D:=diag⁡(ΣΠ)D:=\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma_{\Pi}). Define u:=x−Π¯u:=x-\bar{\Pi} where xj:=Πσ⁡(j),jx_{j}:=\Pi_{\sigma(j),j}. Note Π¯∈ℳ⋆\bar{\Pi}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} by convexity of ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star}, and pointwise 𝔼σ​[uj]=0\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[u_{j}]=0, 𝔼σ​[uj2]=Dj​j\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[u_{j}^{2}]=D_{jj}, and cross-coordinate covariances vanish: 𝔼σ​[uj​uj′]=0\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[u_{j}u_{j^{\prime}}]=0 for j≠j′j\!\neq\!j^{\prime} by independence of σ⁡(j),σ⁡(j′)\sigma(j),\sigma(j^{\prime}).

Generic upper bound.

By Prop. 3.8 with reference r=Π¯r=\bar{\Pi}, ε⋆≤‖u‖2\varepsilon^{\star}\leq\|u\|_{2}, so 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]≤𝔼σ​[‖u‖22]=∑jDj​j=tr⁡(D)\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\|u\|_{2}^{2}]=\sum_{j}D_{jj}=\mathrm{tr}(D).

Equality case (κR=1\kappa_{R}=1).

If ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} contains a single equality aR⊤​r=bRa_{R}^{\top}r=b_{R} binding at the projection (and no other constraint is active locally), the projection has the closed form Π⋆​(x)=x−aR⊤​x−bR‖aR‖2​aR\Pi^{\star}(x)=x-\frac{a_{R}^{\top}x-b_{R}}{\|a_{R}\|^{2}}a_{R}, giving ε⋆=|aR⊤​x−bR|/‖aR‖\varepsilon^{\star}=|a_{R}^{\top}x-b_{R}|/\|a_{R}\|. Since Π¯∈ℳ⋆\bar{\Pi}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star} satisfies aR⊤​Π¯=bRa_{R}^{\top}\bar{\Pi}=b_{R}, we have aR⊤​x−bR=aR⊤​ua_{R}^{\top}x-b_{R}=a_{R}^{\top}u, so ε⋆2=(aR⊤​u)2/‖aR‖2\varepsilon^{\star 2}=(a_{R}^{\top}u)^{2}/\|a_{R}\|^{2}. Taking expectation, 𝔼σ​[(aR⊤​u)2]=aR⊤​D​aR\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(a_{R}^{\top}u)^{2}]=a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R} (cross-terms vanish), so 𝔼σ​[(ε⋆)2]=aR⊤​D​aR/‖aR‖2\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[(\varepsilon^{\star})^{2}]=a_{R}^{\top}Da_{R}/\|a_{R}\|^{2}.

Inequality case with boundary Π¯\bar{\Pi} (κR=12\kappa_{R}=\tfrac{1}{2}).

If the binding constraint at the projection is an inequality aR⊤​r≤bRa_{R}^{\top}r\leq b_{R} with aR⊤​Π¯=bRa_{R}^{\top}\bar{\Pi}=b_{R} (boundary), the single-halfspace projection gives ε⋆=(aR⊤​u)+/‖aR‖\varepsilon^{\star}=(a_{R}^{\top}u)_{+}/\|a_{R}\|. Appendix N Planner-style routing simulation: per-question detail

We report all 100100 live-style partition forecasting questions used in the planner-style routing simulation (Section 4). Each row gives the partition label, the number of outcomes mm, the per-outcome marginal returned by the randomly-assigned specialist LLM (LLM key: C=Claude-Haiku-4.5, M=GPT-5.4-mini, N=GPT-5.4-nano, L=Llama-3.3-70b), the resulting partition mass ∑ipi\sum_{i}p_{i}, and the compositional residual ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}. All four specialist clients ran with K=8K{=}8 verbalized-probability samples at temperature 0.70.7; each received its assigned outcome as an isolated single-question prompt with no context about the partition or the other outcomes. Master seed 00, sampling without replacement when m≤4m\!\leq\!4. Total cost: ≈2,400\approx\!2{,}400 LLM calls, ≈$5\approx\!\$5, ≈35\approx\!35 minutes wall-clock. Rows are sorted by descending ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} so the worst cases appear first.

Worst-case anatomy.

The largest residual (ε⋆=0.749\varepsilon^{\star}=0.749) is the “Largest US AI startup IPO 2026” partition (four sectoral outcomes: infrastructure, model, applications, other). Three of the four assigned specialists privately quote P⁡(their sector)>0.5P(\text{their sector})>0.5 (the fourth is at 0.390.39); collectively the specialists over-allocate, with assigned masses summing to 2.502.50. Each marginal is locally well-calibrated for the single Bernoulli the specialist was asked, but no specialist saw that the four sectors tile the field; as a result, the assembled system quotes 250%250\% probability mass. Simplex projection reduces the quote to a proper distribution in closed form, eliminating the exposure to QP-tolerance. ML-benchmark partitions (Top MMLU, ε⋆=0.65\varepsilon^{\star}{=}0.65; SWE-Bench Verified, 0.540.54; HumanEval+, 0.470.47; GPQA, 0.460.46) form a coherent high-residual cluster: in each, four specialists are assigned to one candidate model organization, and the specialists collectively over-allocate; masses sum to ∼2.0\sim\!2.0 even when only one or two specialists are above 0.50.5 individually.

Why some partitions yield near-zero residual.

The five smallest residuals (Pulitzer Prize Fiction setting 0.0010.001, Booker Prize nationality 0.0020.002, FDA Alzheimer’s drug action 0.0070.007, GLP-1 label expansion 0.0090.009, leading mobile OS 0.0090.009) share a common structure: the partition either has only two real candidate outcomes, or has a strongly bimodal training-set prior. The single-question marginals then approximately satisfy the partition constraint without any explicit cross-component coordination. The certificate is therefore discriminating rather than uniformly positive: it is positive on novel multi-way partitions and near zero on well-rehearsed ones.

Where context helps most.

The largest drops (iso →\to full) are on partitions where isolated specialists strongly anchor to their assigned outcome with no cross-context knowledge of alternatives: “Largest US AI startup IPO 2026” (→0.120.74\!\to\!0.12), “Top MMLU score, year-end 2026” (→0.050.60\!\to\!0.05), “2026 ACM Turing Award area” (→0.130.63\!\to\!0.13). These are partitions over emerging or specialist-knowledge candidates where the specialist needs to know the alternatives to allocate probability mass appropriately.

Where context hurts.

Eighteen partitions show εfull⋆>εiso⋆\varepsilon^{\star}_{\text{full}}\!>\!\varepsilon^{\star}_{\text{iso}}, predominantly political/economic ones where isolated specialists were already roughly normalised (e.g., 2028 US Presidential winner →0.0220.003\!\to\!0.022, 2026 California gubernatorial party →0.260.10\!\to\!0.26). When isolated estimates already average to ∼1\sim 1, forcing specialists to reason about all alternatives can introduce mass that wasn’t there.

Implication for deployment.

Three regimes emerge: (i) prompt-engineering at fixed owner-selection attenuates the failure mode but bottoms out at ε⋆≈0.08\varepsilon^{\star}\!\approx\!0.08 (essentially the isolated →\to listed step); (ii) tool-using planners reach near-zero residual but pay 55–×7\!\times the naive elicitation budget, with frontier reasoning depth required to close the last ∼0.005\sim\!0.005 that tool-use alone leaves; (iii) hierarchical projection reaches the same near-zero residual at the naive ×m1\!\times\!m elicitation cost, modulo a small QP solve. The geometric repair is therefore the cost-efficient route to coherence when the coupling set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is specifiable; smart-planner integration is the alternative when 𝒞\mathcal{C} is implicit and the planner can infer it through extra delegate calls.

Appendix P Tool-augmented specialist A/B: per-partition detail

We re-run the first 3030 partitions of the case study under a tool-augmented protocol (§4). Each specialist issues exactly one DuckDuckGo web_search call against its assigned outcome text, and the top-five title+snippet results are inserted as context before the specialist emits its K=8K{=}8 verbalized-probability samples. Master seed and assignment are identical to the no-tool first-3030 baseline, so the per-partition Δ​ε⋆=εt⋆−εb⋆\Delta\varepsilon^{\star}=\varepsilon^{\star}_{t}-\varepsilon^{\star}_{b} is a direct A/B. Total cost: ≈720\approx\!720 LLM calls + 9090 search calls, ≈$2\approx\!\$2, ≈25\approx\!25 minutes wall-clock.

Aggregate: mean εb⋆=0.260→εt⋆=0.283\varepsilon^{\star}_{b}=0.260\to\varepsilon^{\star}_{t}=0.283; 20/3020/30 partitions are equal or worse with retrieval, 10/3010/30 are better; mean Δ​ε⋆=+0.023\Delta\varepsilon^{\star}=+0.023. The single largest worsening is “World population, mid-2027” (+0.563+0.563): every specialist’s search returns recent UN bracket estimates around 8.18.1–8.28.2 bn and each anchors near P⁡(their bucket)≈0.7P(\text{their bucket}){\approx}0.7, summing to 2.222.22. The single largest improvement is “2026 Grammy Album of the Year genre” (−0.267-0.267): retrieval surfaces 2026 Grammy nominee distributions that pull every specialist toward a similar partition shape.

Appendix Q Per-specialist residual attribution

For each ensemble bet with ε⋆>10−9\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!10^{-9} (npos=894n_{\text{pos}}\!=\!894 across the 1,876-bet ensemble of §4), we attribute residual mass to each specialist by computing the L2L_{2} norm of the residual vector (x−Π⋆​(x))(x{-}\Pi^{\star}(x)) restricted to the coordinates that specialist owned. The decomposition gives a per-clique credit assignment for which sub-model drives the joint incoherence.

GPT-5.4-mini carries the largest attributed mass per clique among the four mid-tier specialists, consistent with the frontier-panel finding (§5.5) that the GPT-5.5 upgrade reduces magnitude but not prevalence: even with a frontier roster, ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 97.8%97.8\% of the matched partition bets.

Appendix R Trivial vs. hierarchical projection: per-relation gaps

We verify that the closed-form local projections of App. C agree with the iterative Boyle–Dykstra cycle of Theorem 3.10 to numerical precision on the equality-couple relations (negation, partition) and require the cyclic iteration to recover the exact L2L_{2} projection on the inequality-couple relations (conjunction, disjunction), where the Fréchet polytope is not a Cartesian product of half-spaces.

The conjunction/disjunction mean gaps (∼10−3\sim\!10^{-3}) are well below the per-clique ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} magnitudes (0.0580.058–0.1180.118 on these relations, §5.1), so the empirical residuals reported throughout are not artefacts of any approximate projection step; the Dykstra cycle converges to the exact L2L_{2} projection on every clique reported.

Appendix S Causal-mechanism (coupling-visibility) experiment

This appendix supports the coupling-visibility intervention of §5.4.

Sample of partitions.

The 20 partitions are the full planner-harness slate of §5.3; the spec “20 highest-ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star}” selects every partition because the harness has ε⋆>0\varepsilon^{\star}\!>\!0 on 20/2020/20.

Routing.

Held fixed across Blind and Informed at the planner-harness’s chosen specialist-to-outcome assignment per partition. The original planner harness has no random-assignment seeds; the four “seeds” here are independent K=8K\!=\!8 sampling rounds per (partition, condition), giving four paired ε⋆\varepsilon^{\star} values per partition.

Prompts.

Blind is a single-Bernoulli question on the assigned outcome with no partition context. Informed additionally shows the partition label, all sibling outcomes, the explicit ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}\!=\!1 constraint, and the peers’ Blind quotes on the other outcomes. Informed uses Blind quotes from the same seed as context, so the two conditions are tightly paired within a (partition, seed) cell.

Aggregate result.

Mean paired Δ​ε⋆=εBlind⋆−εInformed⋆=+0.221\Delta\varepsilon^{\star}=\varepsilon^{\star}_{\textsc{Blind}}{-}\varepsilon^{\star}_{\textsc{Informed}}=+0.221 (95%95\% paired-bootstrap CI [+0.173,+0.270][+0.173,+0.270]; Wilcoxon W=257W{=}257, p=×10−10p\!=\!2.6\!\times\!10^{-10}; npairs=77/80n_{\text{pairs}}\!=\!77/80 cells surviving parsing). 16/2016/20 partitions improve under Informed, 1/201/20 unchanged, 3/203/20 worsened. The three worsening partitions (Δ<0\Delta\!<\!0) are non-payoff multi-way forecasts where Blind specialists were already roughly normalised; Informed can introduce mass that the isolated quotes did not have. This matches the LLM-side mitigations result (§5.2): prompt-based fixes can harm already-coherent quotes, and the geometric certificate gates them.
